statement:
This problem extends the idea of a cylinder as a spring and gives you some practice in working with formulas that are given in the problem. You should come away "half way" understanding the formulas. That is, you should be able to make some inferences about them needed to solve the problem, but should not expect to understand everything about where the formulas come from. This mode of reasoning about formulas is common in olympiad physics.

**a)** Suppose a cylinder has length $$L_0,$$ radius $$R_0,$$ and Young's modulus $$Y,$$ all when under no stress. If the cylinder is subjected to a uniform tension $$T,$$ it stretches, and its volume may increase from $$V_0 = \pi R_0^2 L_0$$ to $$V(T) = \left(1+\lambda(T)\right) V_0.$$ Assuming the radius stays constant as the cylinder stretches, find $$\lambda(T).$$

**b)** Most cylinders, when stretched, do not maintain constant radius. A more realistic assumption for certain materials is that the volume of the cylinder does not change at all when stretched. Suppose we have such a cylinder and we stretch it so that its length $$L$$ increases: $$ L \to (1+\alpha) L.$$ Then the radius also changes $$ R \to (1+\beta) R.$$

Suppose the change in length is very small, so $$\alpha \ll 1.$$ Find $$\beta$$ as a function of $$\alpha.$$

Your answer should be approximate for finite $$\alpha,$$ but exact in the limit $$\alpha \to 0.$$

**c)** The ratio $$-\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}$$ is called **Poisson's ratio**. A common symbol for Poisson's ratio is $$ u.$$ What is Poisson's ratio for the material in part (a) of this question? What is it for the material in part (b) of this question?

**d)** The material in part (b), which strongly resists changes to its volume, has a very high **bulk modulus** $$B.$$ The material in part (a) has a very low bulk modulus. One of the following formulas gives Poisson's ratio as a function of bulk modulus and Young's modulus. Which one?

\begin{aligned} u & = \dfrac{3B - Y}{6B} \\ \vspace{2pt} \\ u & = \dfrac{Y - 3B}{3B} \\ \vspace{2pt} \\ u & = \dfrac{3B - Y}{6Y} \\ \vspace{2pt} \\ u & = \dfrac{3Y - B}{6Y} \\ \vspace{2pt} \\ u & = \dfrac{3B - Y}{3B} \end{aligned}

statement:
A zero effective length spring (ZLS) is a spring for which the force is proportional to the spring's length, $$F = kL$$ for $$L>L_0,$$ where $$L_0$$ is the minimal length of the spring as well as its unstretched length. The figure shows the relation between the force $$F$$ and the spring length $$L$$ for a ZLS, where the slope of the line is the spring constant $$k.$$

A ZLS is useful in seismography and allows very accurate measurement of changes in the gravitational acceleration $$g.$$ Here, we shall consider a homogenous ZLS whose weight $$Mg$$ exceeds $$kL_0.$$ We define a corresponding dimensionless ratio, $$\alpha = kL_0/(Mg) < 1$$ to characterize the relative softness of the spring. The toy known as a "slinky" may be (but is not necessarily) such a ZLS.

**a)** Consider a segment of length $$\Delta l$$ of the unstretched ZLS which is then stretched by a force $$F$$ under weightless conditions. What is the new length $$\Delta y$$ of this segment as a function of $$F, \Delta l,$$ and the parameters of the spring?

**b)** For a segment of length $$\Delta l,$$ calculate the work $$\Delta W$$ required to stretch it from its original length to a length $$\Delta y.$$

Throughout part (c), we will denote a point on the spring by its distance $$0 \le l \le L_0$$ from the bottom of the spring when it is unstretched. In particular, for every point on the spring, $$l$$ remains unchanged as the spring stretches.

**c)** Suppose that we hang the spring by its top end, so that it stretches under its own weight. What is the total length $$H$$ of the suspended spring in equilibrium? Express your answer in terms of $$L_0$$ and $$\alpha.$$

statement:
The following is a problem based on IPhO, 1990 (Netherlands). However, the analysis presented by the Netherlanders was actually incorrect! Here, we'll try to replicate what they thought the right approach was, then see if we can find where they went wrong.

If the Earth didn't rotate, it would be almost a perfect sphere (if we ignore mountains, which are relatively small). However, due to its rotation, the Earth bulges out at the center. Here we will calculate the size of the Earth's equatorial bulge.

Let the distance from the center of the Earth to one of the poles be $$r_p$$ and the distance from the center of the Earth to the equator be $$r_e.$$

The following information is useful: \begin{aligned} \text{mass of Earth} & = 5.97 \times 10^{24} \;\mathrm{kg}\\ \text{radius of Earth} & = 6.37 \times 10^6 \;\mathrm{m} \\ \text{Newton's gravitational constant} & = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{N \cdot m^2 \cdot kg^{-2}} \end{aligned}

**a)** Above pressures of about $$1 \;\mathrm{GPa},$$ rocks and metals cannot hold their solid shape. They can be thought of as essentially liquids at these pressures. Can the rotating Earth be thought of as a liquid?

**b)** In a frame co-rotating with the Earth, the centrifugal force on an object of mass $$m$$ can be thought of as the gradient of a potential energy, $$U(r),$$ where $$r$$ is the distance from the axis of rotation. Find $$U(r).$$

**c)** The Earth's shape should be an equipotential surface in the rotating frame. This means that if we took a small rock of mass $$m$$ at the equator and moved it to a pole, its potential energy wouldn't change.

The rock's gravitational potential energy at the equator is higher than at the pole by approximately $$mgh,$$ where $$h = r_e - r_p.$$ So this must be balanced by the centrifugal potential. Use this to calculate $$r_e - r_p$$ for Earth.

**d)** On Earth, $$r_e - r_p \approx 21 \;\mathrm{km}.$$ Does this agree with the theory derived in part (c)? If not, what is the major source of error in the calculation?

statement:
This problem and the next one continue problem 8 from week 1 on a zero-length spring. You may wish to review that problem before working this one.

A zero effective length spring (ZLS) is a spring for which the force is proportional to the spring's length, $$F = kL$$ for $$L>L_0,$$ where $$L_0$$ is the minimal length of the spring as well as its unstretched length. The figure shows the relation between the force $$F$$ and the spring length $$L$$ for a ZLS, where the slope of the line is the spring constant $$k.$$

A ZLS is useful in seismography and allows very accurate measurement of changes in the gravitational acceleration $$g.$$ Here, we shall consider a homogenous ZLS whose weight $$Mg$$ exceeds $$kL_0.$$ We define a corresponding dimensionless ratio, $$\alpha = kL_0/Mg < 1$$ to characterize the relative softness of the spring. The toy known as a "slinky" may be (but is not necessarily) such a ZLS.

Throughout this question, we will denote a point on the spring by its distance $$0 \le \ell \le L_0$$ from the bottom of the spring when it is unstretched. In particular, for every point on the spring, $$\ell$$ remains unchanged as the spring stretches.

Experiments show that when the spring is hung at rest and then released, it gradually contracts from the top, while the lower part remains stationary (see Figure 2 below).

As time advances, the contracting part moves as a solid chunk and accumulates additional turns of the spring, while the stationary part becomes shorter. Every point on the spring begins to move only when the moving part reaches it. The bottom end of the spring starts moving only when the spring is fully collapsed and reaches its unstretched length $$L_0.$$ After that, the contracted spring continues falling straight downwards, without tumbling, as a rigid body under the influence of gravity.

In the remaining parts of the question, you are asked to base your solution on this described model. You may neglect air resistance, but you are not allowed to neglect $$L_0.$$

**a)** The spring is held from its top and released. Calculate the time $$t_c$$ from the moment the spring is released to the moment it fully collapses back to its minimal length $$L_0.$$ Express your answer in terms of $$L_0, g,$$ and $$\alpha.$$

Compute the numerical value for $$t_c$$ for a spring with $$k = 1.02 \;\mathrm{N/m},$$ $$L_0 = 0.055 \;\mathrm{m},$$ and $$M = 0.201 \;\mathrm{kg},$$ while taking $$g$$ to be $$9.80 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

The "Tennis Racket Theorem" describes a striking effect of rigid bodies rotating freely in space, illustrated below:

Recall that in the handout, we briefly discussed the three principal axes for the rotation of a rigid body about its center. The "flipping" behavior seen in the gif above occurs when rotating about the principal axis $$I_2$$ with a moment of inertia in between the other moments of inertia of the other two axes.

Although most explanations of this effect involve complicated analysis, in 2011 mathematician Terry Tao posted a simple explanation of the effect to the website MathOverflow. The YouTube channel "Veritasium" recently created a video illustrating this explanation.

The video is available (https://youtu.be/1VPfZ_XzisU); it may help to visualize the effects we'll analyze. The video is, however, incomplete; this problem will fill in some details.

Consider a cross made of two massless sticks of length $$2\ell.$$ The intersection between the sticks is located at the origin. One stick lies along the $$x$$ axis and the other lies along the $$y$$ axis.

The stick lying along the $$y$$ axis has two point masses attached to it; one at either end. The masses are each $$m.$$

The stick lying along the $$x$$ axis has two point masses attached to it as well; again one at each end. The masses are each $$M,$$ and we assume $$M \gg m.$$

**a)** Find the moments of inertia $$I_x, I_y,$$ and $$I_z$$ of the cross about each coordinate axis. Which axis is the intermediate axis?

**b)** We imagine the cross begins rotating about the $$y$$ axis with angular frequency $$\omega$$ in the direction such that the $$y$$ component of angular momentum is positive. (And the $$x$$ and $$z$$ components of angular momentum are zero.) Next, we transform into a frame rotating in the same sense, so that the cross is stationary. Find the forces on each mass in this frame.

**c)** The rotating frame can be described with coordinates $$x', y', z'$$ obeying \begin{aligned} y' & = y \\ x' & = x\cos\omega t + z \sin\omega t \\ z' & = z\cos\omega t - x \sin\omega t \\ \end{aligned}

If the cross is perfectly aligned with the $$y$$ axis, then in the rotating frame, we can have equilibrium, and no "flipping" motion occurs. Perfect alignment is never completely possible, though.

Suppose that the cross is very slightly misaligned, so that the stick along the $$y'$$ axis is actually inclined to the $$y'$$ axis by some angle $$\phi.$$

Find angular acceleration of the disk as a function of $$\phi,$$ and thereby find an equation of motion for $$\phi.$$ For this part of the problem, neglect Coriolis forces.

**d)** Suppose there were another T-shaped piece, like the one in the gif, but twice as big in all dimensions and the same density. How would the time between its flipping back and forth compare to the time between flipping back and forth for the piece in the gif? The video mentions a concern that Earth could flip upside down. If it were to do so based on the equation of motion you derived in part (c), estimate (to order of magnitude only) how long that would take.

**e)** The analysis above seems to explain why the cross would flip directions, then flip back, while spinning. But what if the cross were originally spinning around the $$x$$ axis? We could make exactly the same argument as before, imagining a slight rotation about the $$y$$ axis which, due to centrifugal forces, makes the cross flip back and forth. But this is not observed - it's only spinning around the $$y$$ axis that leads to instability. Why isn't spinning around the $$x$$ axis similarly unstable?

(Your answer will have an undetermined coefficient.)

statement:
Galaxies are a large collection of stars and gas that are held together by their own gravity. The stars and gas in a spiral galaxy trace out circular orbits around the centre of the galaxy. A schematic of a spiral galaxy, the Milky Way, can be seen below.

statement:
In this problem, we'll get more familiar with the **virial theorem**. The virial theorem is proved in the handout with an example problem, and here we'll take another perspective. We'll return to the virial theorem one more time when we study quantum mechanics in our final problem set.

The virial theorem for Newtonian gravity states that for any system of particles that is gravitationally bound (i.e. they interact via gravity, and the particles can't shoot off to infinity), $$\langle T \rangle = -\left\langle \dfrac{U}{2}\right\rangle $$ where $$T$$ is the total kinetic energy of the system and $$U$$ the total potential energy. The brackets $$(\langle \; \rangle)$$ indicate a time average over a very long time, e.g. $$ \langle T \rangle = \lim_{\tau\to\infty} \dfrac{1}{\tau} \int_0^\tau T(t)\mathrm{d}t.$$

**a)** Show that the virial theorem holds for a particle in a circular orbit around a star. You may ignore any effect of the particle on the star.

**b)** Now show it again, but this time, don't assume that the particle is much less massive than the star.

Next, we'll work through a proof of the virial theorem.

**c)** Define the following quantity $$G$$ as the "virial". $$ G = \sum_i \vec{p}_i \cdot \vec{r}_i.$$ Here, we are imagining a system of particles indexed by $$i.$$ $$\vec{p}_i$$ is the momentum of the $$i$$th particle and $$\vec{r}_i$$ is the position of the $$i$$th particle.

Express the time derivative $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}G}{\mathrm{d}t}$$ in terms of the total kinetic energy of the system and a sum over a term involving the net force on the $$i$$th particle, $$\vec{F}_i,$$ and $$\vec{r}_i.$$

**d)** Imagine watching the system for a very long time. What is the time-average of $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}G}{\mathrm{d}t}$$ in the limit where the time you spend watching the system goes to infinity? You should be able to answer this without doing any calculation.

**e)** In part (c), you derived an equation for $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}G}{\mathrm{d}t},$$ and you now know the value of the long-time average of quantity. Use this to find a relation between the long-time average of the system's kinetic energy and the long-time average of a quantity involving a sum over a function of $$\vec{F}_i$$ and $$\vec{r}_i.$$

To make sure you're on the right track, at this point you should have,

$$2 \langle T \rangle = \left\langle \sum_i \vec{F}_i \cdot \vec{r}_i \right\rangle.$$

You should now have something that's starting to look at bit like the virial theorem, but it involves a sum over particles involving forces and positions instead of simply the potential energy of the system. However, forces and positions, when combined, are related to potential energy, so our remaining job is to flesh out this relationship.

**f)** $$\vec{F}_i$$ is the net force on particle $$i.$$ Write this as a sum over all the particles $$j$$ not equal to $$i.$$ Rewrite your expression from part (e) using a double sum over $$i$$ and $$j eq i.$$

**g)** Consider two terms from the sum in part (f), one for $$i = 1, j = 2$$ and one for $$i = 2, j=1.$$ Then $$\vec{F}_{ij}$$ in the first case is the same as $$\vec{F}_{ji}$$ in the second. Use this fact to rewrite the sum to sum over $$i$$ and $$j < i$$ so that the sum evaluates to the same thing as before. Apply Newton's third law and simplify the result as much as possible.

An alternative way to communicate this instruction is: Split the sum into one for $$j < i$$ and one for $$j > i$$. Then reverse $$i$$ and $$j$$ in one of the sums to combine them back into a single sum for $$j < i$$."

You should find

$$ \langle T\rangle = -\dfrac12 \left\langle \sum_i\sum_{j < i} (\vec{F}_{ji}\cdot \left(\vec{r}_i -\vec{r}_j\right) \right\rangle.$$

**h)** Suppose the potential energy between any pair of particles is $$U_{ij} = k r_{ij}^n$$ where $$r_{ij}$$ is the distance between the particles. Find $$\vec{F}_{ij}$$ in terms of $$U_{ij}$$ and $$\hat{r}_{ij}$$ and use this to simplify your equation from part (g). You should now have a complete proof of the virial theorem.

**a)** A particle is a distance $$r$$ from the sun and moves at speed $$v.$$ Its velocity is perpendicular to the vector from the sun to the particle's position. On the other side of the sun, the particle's distance from the sun is $$r'.$$ Find $$r'.$$

You should find that there are no allowed values of $$r'$$ for certain combinations of $$r$$ and $$v.$$ Find the condition on $$r$$ and $$v$$ such that $$r'$$ exists, and give an interpretation to your result.

---------------

In this problem, we'll explore the concept of an **effective potential**. This concept came up in the handout in the proof of Kepler's first law, but we didn't explicitly label it there. After you solve this problem, you might want to revisit the proof of Kepler's first law given in the handout to see how the effective potential was used.

Revisit the calculation in part (a).

If you try to make $$r'$$ smaller than the correct value and calculate $$v'$$ via conservation of energy, you'll find that the particle's angular momentum has decreased from the initial position of $$r$$ with speed $$v.$$ In other words, the particle can't get too close to the sun due to conservation of angular momentum. It's almost as if angular momentum creates a push that shoves particles out from the sun, countering the attractive force of gravity.

This is the idea that the effective potential formalizes.

**b)** In polar coordinates the velocity of a particle has two component, $$v_r$$ and $$v_\theta.$$ Find the energy of the particle in terms of these components and $$r, G,m,$$ and $$M.$$

**c)** Find the angular momentum of the particle using the variables as in part (b).

**d)** Use the result of part (c) to eliminate $$v_\theta$$ from part (b). You should find that the energy is the same as if the potential energy were $$V = U_{e} + U.$$ What is $$U_{e}?$$ The name for $$V$$ is the **effective potential**.

To check your answer, you should find

$$U_{e} = \dfrac{L^2}{2mr^2}.$$

**e)** A circular orbit is one where $$r$$ is constant. This means that $$V$$ is minimized at the correct $$r.$$ Use this fact to find the radius $$r_0$$ of a circular orbit under Newtonian gravity for a fixed $$L.$$ Verify that your result is correct by comparing it to a straightforward calculation based on Newton's laws.

**f)** Find the angular frequency of small oscillations about about $$r_0.$$ Is your answer what you expect based on Kepler's laws?

**g)** A masses $$m$$ is attached to the end of a string, which extends through a hole in a frictionless table. An external agent applies a constant tension $$T$$ to the end of the string hanging through the hole. The mass rotates around the table at an angular velocity $$\Omega$$ such that its distance from the hole is constant. Next, the mass is given a small radial velocity. Find the angular frequency $$\omega$$ of oscillations the mass's distance from the hole in terms of $$\Omega.$$ How does your result compare to what you found in the previous parts of this problem? What does this imply about whether the orbit is "closed" (I.E. the mass goes back to the same state after one orbit)?

**h)** Suppose that a particle is subjected to the central potential $$U = cr^n$$ With $$n$$ an integer. Throughout the rest of this problem, we will determine for which values of $$n$$ orbits are closed.

Our first step in this proof is: suppose the particle orbits with angular frequency $$\Omega,$$ then is given a small push in the radial direction. For what $$n$$ does the particle's distance from the center of its orbit oscillate?

For what $$n$$ does the particle return to its original state after one orbit, given these infinitesimal perturbations?

To check your progress, you should find the $$n$$ for which the particle returns to its original state after one orbit, given an infinitesimal push, are

\[ n = -1, 2, 7, 14, \ldots , k^2 - 2 , \ldots .\] for any integer $$k.$$

**i)** Our work in part (h) shows that for most potentials, orbits are not closed. It turns out, though, that even most of the potentials that survived our test in part (h) do not yield closed orbits when we allow the oscillations about a circular orbit to be any more than infinitesimal. Our goal in the rest of the problem is to determine which of the potentials that survived the test in part (h) truly give closed orbits. The result is called **Bertrand's Theorem**. (Although in reality, Bertrand's theorem is slightly stronger because it doesn't assume the potential is a power law where the exponent is an integer.)

In part (h), there should be both positive and negative $$n$$ among your answers. Why do we only need to focus on the positive $$n$$ for the rest of the problem? Among the positive $$n$$ values you found, are there any you know do yield closed orbits?

In order to evaluate positive $$n,$$ we'll do the following intermediate calculation:

For the small perturbations studied in part (h), find the angle between the position vector of the planet when it is furthest from the center of the orbit and when it is closest to the center of the orbit. This is called the **apsidal angle**.

In what follows, we'll assume that the apsidal angle does not vary depending on the orbital parameters. (This is true and can be shown via some manipulations of the equations of motion that we aren't going to bother with, but any online derivation of Bertrand's theorem will include them.)

In the final part of the problem, we'll use another line of reasoning to determine what the apsidal angle must be, assuming $$n>0$$ and the orbit is closed. Then only those $$n$$ with the correct apsidal angle can give closed orbits.

**j)** This final part of the problem is somewhat technical, but will allow us to determine the allowed apsidal angles in closed orbits with $$n > 0$$ using some tricks.

The main idea is that we want to turn our equations into something that looks like a system we understand: the harmonic oscillator. We have an understanding of the energy of our system based on the effective potential, and we will try to manipulate that energy to look like the energy in a harmonic oscillator.

The effective potential includes the angular momentum term $$\dfrac{L}{mr^2}.$$ This doesn't look like the potential energy of a harmonic oscillator, $$U = \dfrac12 kx^2.$$ But we can make it look like the harmonic oscillator by defining $$x = \dfrac{1}{r}$$ and turning the equation for energy in the orbit into an equation for $$x.$$

Write an equation for energy conservation in an orbit using $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}, L, m, r, c,$$ and $$n.$$

Because we are interested in the apsidal angle, we want to study the variation in $$r$$ over $$\theta$$ instead of $$t,$$ so rewrite the equation using $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}\theta}, \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t}, L, m, r, c,n,$$ and $$E,$$ the total energy of the orbit. Then eliminate $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t}$$ using $$L, m,$$ and $$r.$$

Now switch to the variable $$x = \dfrac{1}{r}.$$ If all this went well, you should have

$$ \dfrac12 \dfrac{L^2}{m} \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 + \dfrac{L^2}{2m}x^2 + \dfrac{c}{x^n} = E.$$

This looks kinda of like a harmonic oscillator, but it has that extra term

$$\dfrac{c}{x^n}.$$

We need another trick to deal with the effect of this term. That trick will be to consider the limiting case where the energy of the orbit goes to infinity.

Let $$E \to \infty.$$ At typical $$x$$ values, what happens to that extra term, as compared to the rest of the potential? At what $$x$$ does the term still matter? Argue that the potential energy can be thought of, in this limit, as a harmonic oscillator potential energy with a key modification about where the particle is allowed to go inside the potential. What is that modification?

Based on that modification, what is the angular frequency of $$x(\theta)?$$ What does this imply about the apsidal angle? Finally, based on all the above, for what values of $$n$$ are orbits closed?

If you work through all of this, you'll have proved a simplified version of Bertrand's theorem! Enjoy working through the problem and share your progress on the message board.

A satellite in low-Earth orbit experiences a small frictional force, the drag force, because although the air is very thin hundreds of kilometers up, it still exists.

**a)** Does the drag force result in satellites speeding up or slowing down relative to the center of Earth? Answer this question without performing any calculations.

We assume that the drag force may be written $$ \vec{F} = -k\vec{v}.$$

**b)** What are the dimensions of $$k?$$ If $$k$$ depends on the satellite's cross-sectional area $$A,$$ the air density $$\rho,$$ and the speed $$v,$$ what is a plausible formula for $$k?$$

**c)** A satellite orbits at altitude $$h = 160 \;\mathrm{km}.$$ The air density is $$\rho = 10^{-9} \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$ The speed is $$v = 8 \;\mathrm{km/s}.$$ The satellite cross-sectional area is $$A = 1 \;\mathrm{m}^2.$$ Its mass is $$100 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ What is the ratio of the satellite's acceleration due to friction to the satellite's acceleration due to gravity?

**d)** Assume that the satellite's orbit is almost circular. Find the velocity of the satellite as a function of time over times short enough that the satellite's height about Earth does not vary significantly. Does your answer confirm what you found in part (a)? If not, you may wish to revise your answer to that part of the problem. You may give only a symbolic answer to this problem; plugging in the numbers is not necessary.

A uniform chain of mass $$m$$ and length $$\ell$$ is sliding off a rough table. At time $$t$$ length $$x$$ lies over the edge of the table. **b)** Assuming that the chain accelerates in such a way that the picture above remains accurate (except that $$x$$ changes), find the equation of motion for the chain.

**c)** Find the solution to the equation of motion in (b) using the initial condition that the chain was placed at the maximum $$x$$ discovered in part (a), then given a small initial velocity $$v_0$$ in the direction towards the edge of the table.

statement:
The phenomenon of creaking is very common, and can be found in doors, closets, chalk squeaking on a blackboard, playing a violin, new shoes, car brakes and other systems from everyday life. A similar phenomenon can cause violent earthquakes with a period of several decades. The physical mechanism for creaking is based on elasticity combined with the difference between the static and the kinetic friction coefficients. In this question, we will study this mechanism and its application to the case of an opening door.

Consider the following system:

We would like to understand why this setup supports two different forms of motion:

1. The friction is always kinetic. This is known as the **pure slip** mode. 2. Kinetic and static friction alternate. This is known as a **stick-slip** mode. Stick-slip motion is the source of the creaking sound commonly encountered.

**a)** Consider the case where at the initial time $$t = 0,$$ the box slides on the floor with velocity $$v_0,$$ and the spring's tension exactly balances the kinetic friction. Assume $$0 < v_0 < u.$$ The **spring's elongation** $$x$$ will oscillate as a function of $$t.$$

Find the period $$T_0$$ and the amplitude $$A$$ of these oscillations.

Sketch a qualitative graph of the spring's elongation $$x(t)$$ for $$0 < t < 3T_0.$$

**b)** Now, consider the case where at $$t=0$$ the box is at rest, while the initial spring elongation $$x$$ is the same as in part (a). Sketch a qualitative graph of the velocity $$v(t)$$ of the box with respect to the floor for $$0 < t < 3T,$$ where $$T$$ is the (new) period of the oscillations $$x(t).$$ Motion to the right corresponds to a positive sign of $$v.$$ Indicate approximately on your graph the horizontal line $$v = u.$$

**c)** For the initial conditions of part (b), find the time-averaged value $$\bar{x}$$ of the spring's elongation after a sufficiently long time has passed.

**d)** For the conditions of part (b), find the period $$T$$ of the oscillations $$x(t).$$

statement:
This problem continues the previous one on creaking.

A door hinge is a hollow, open-ended metal cylinder with radius $$r,$$ height $$h,$$ and thickness $$\Delta r.$$ The lower end of the cylinder lies on a metal base attached to the wall (the area of contact is a ring of radius $$r.)$$ The static and kinetic friction coefficients between the cylinder and its base are $$\mu_s$$ and $$\mu_k$$ respectively, which $$\mu_k < \mu_s.$$ The upper end of the cylinder is attached to the door, which can be regarded as perfectly rigid. A typical door hangs on two or three such hinges, but its weight is concentrated on only one of them - this is the hinge that will creak. The cylinder of that hinge presses down on its metal base with the weight of the entire door, whose mass is $$M.$$

The cylinder is not a perfectly rigid body - it can twist tangentially without changing its overall form, so that vertical line segments become tilted with a small angle $$\alpha.$$ (Shown on the right.) the elastic force on a small area element $$\mathrm{d}S$$ of the base due to this deformation is given by $$\mathrm{d}F = G\alpha \mathrm{d}S,$$ where $$G$$ is a material property known as the shear modulus. Use the values \begin{aligned} r & = 5 \;\mathrm{mm} \\ h & = 3 \;\mathrm{cm} \\ \Delta r & = 1 \;\mathrm{mm}\\ \mu_s & = 0.75\\ \mu_k & = 0.55\\ G & = 8 \times 10^{10} \;\mathrm{Pa} \\ M & = 30 \;\mathrm{kg} \\ g & = 9.8 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}. \end{aligned}

You may use the approximation $$\Delta r \ll r.$$

**a)** We start rotating the door very slowly from the equilibrium (zero torque). For small rotation angles, obtain an expression for the torsion coefficient $$\kappa = \dfrac{\tau}{\theta},$$ where $$\tau$$ is the torque which must be applied to rotate the door by an angle $$\theta.$$

**b)** At very low angular velocity, when a transition from stick to slip occurs, a sound pulse is emitted. Find the angular velocity $$\Omega$$ of the door for which the frequency of these pulses enters the audible range at $$f = 20 \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ Assume the frequency $$f_0$$ of pure-slip oscillations in the hinge is much higher: $$f_0 \gg f.$$ Provide an expression and a numerical result.

statement:
Here are three short problems to use to practice error propagation.

**a)** A simple pendulum consists of a string of length $$\ell \pm \delta \ell$$ connected to a mass $$m \pm \delta m.$$ Estimate the accuracy to which local gravitational acceleration can be measured if the period is known to very good accuracy.

Estimate the largest acceptable relative error in the period that will negligibly affect the results.

Estimate the maximum amplitude such that the formula for the small-amplitude period can be used while negligibly affecting the results. You may need to know $$\sin\theta \approx \theta - \dfrac{\theta^3}{6}.$$

Estimate the minimum mass of the string such that it needs to be accounted for in the calculations.

If the mass is a sphere connected to the string and $$\ell$$ the distance from the top of the string to the center of the sphere, estimate the minimum radius of the sphere such that it needs to be accounted for.

**b)**

In 1849, Fizeau devised the first accurate method for determining the speed of light.

Fizeau's experiment is illustrated below.

The experiment used a rotated wheel with square teeth. Light travelled from a gap between two adjacent teeth to a mirror $$8633 \;\mathrm{m}$$ away and was reflected back to the wheel.

Meanwhile, the adjacent tooth had replaced the gap and blocked out the returning beam.

Fizeau used a wheel with 720 teeth and a rotation rate of 12.6 revolutions per second. Determine the value of $$c$$ obtained.

If the rotation rate was accurate to $$4\%,$$ find the accuracy of his result.

**c)** Two students are asked to measure the rate of emission of alpha particles from a certain radioactive sample. Student A watches for 2 minutes and counts 32 particles. Student В watches for 1 hour and counts 786 particles. (The sample decays slowly enough that the expected rate of emission can be assumed to be constant during the measurements.) i. What is the uncertainty in Student A's result, 32, for the number of particles emitted in 2 minutes? ii. What is the uncertainty in Student B's result, 786, for the number of particles emitted in 1 hour? iii. Each student now divides their count by their number of minutes to find the rate of emission in particles per minute. Assuming the times, 2 min and 60 min, have negligible uncertainty, what are the two students' answers for the rate, with their uncertainties?

statement:
This problem has more practice with error propagation.

**a)** A block slides down an inclined plane with angle $$\theta.$$ The block slides a distance $$L,$$ starting from rest. The coefficient of friction between the block and plane is $$\mu < \tan\theta.$$ The time for the block to slide down the plane is $$T.$$

Measuring these values, an experimenter finds \begin{aligned} \theta & = 30 \pm 1^\circ \\ \mu & = .20 \pm 0.01 \\ T & = 1.1 \pm 0.1 \;\mathrm{s}\\ L & = 2.0 \pm 0.1 \;\mathrm{m} \\ \end{aligned}

Find uncertainty in local gravitational acceleration that can be deduced from the above information.

**b)** The normal average incidence of a certain kind of cancer has been established as 2 cases per 10,000 people per year. The suspicion has been aired that a certain town (population 20,000) suffers a high incidence of this cancer because of a nearby chemical dump. To test this claim, a reporter investigates the town's records for the past 4 years and finds 20 cases of the cancer. He calculates that the expected number and concludes that the observed rate is 25% more than expected. How did he arrive at this figure? Is he justified in claiming that this result proves that the town has a higher than normal rate for this cancer?

To answer this question, you may want to model occurrences of cancer in the same way we model other counting events.

**c)** If I have measured the radius of a sphere to be $$2.0 \pm 0.1 \;\mathrm{m},$$ what should I report for the sphere's volume? Repeat this question with your own made-up measurement of the volume, and find how the radius should be reported.

desc: Here is some more practice with error propagation. **a)** Suppose two independent measurements are made of some quantity, $$x.$$ The results are \begin{aligned} x_1 \pm \delta x_1 \\ x_2 \pm \delta x_2 \end{aligned} It is desired to get the best-possible estimate of $$x.$$ This…
statement:
Here is some more practice with error propagation.

**a)** Suppose two independent measurements are made of some quantity, $$x.$$ The results are \begin{aligned} x_1 \pm \delta x_1 \\ x_2 \pm \delta x_2 \end{aligned}

It is desired to get the best-possible estimate of $$x.$$ This will be done using a weighted average, $$x = \alpha x_1 + (1-\alpha) x_2.$$

Find the value of $$\alpha$$ that minimizes the uncertainty in $$x.$$

**b)** In his famous experiment with electrons, J.J. Thomson measured the "charge to mass ratio", $$r = e/m,$$ where $$e$$ is the electron's charge and $$m$$ its mass. A modern classroom version of this experiment finds the ratio $$r$$ by accelerating electrons through a voltage $$V$$ and then bending them in a magnetic field. The ratio $$r = e/m$$ is given by the formula $$r = \dfrac{125}{32 \mu_0^2 N^2} \dfrac{D^2 V}{d^2 I^2}.$$

In this equation, $$\mu_0$$ is the permeability constant of the vacuum (equal to $$4\pi \times 10^{-7} \;\mathrm{N/A^2}$$ exactly) and $$N$$ is the number of turns in the coil that produces the magnetic field. $$D$$ is the diameter of the field of coils. $$V$$ is the voltage that accelerates the electrons. $$d$$ is the diameter of the electrons' curved path. $$I$$ is the current in the field coils.

A student makes the following measurements: \begin{aligned} N & = 72 \\ D & = 661 \pm 2 \;\mathrm{mm} \\ V & = 45.0 \pm 0.2 \;\mathrm{V} \\ d & = 91.4 \pm 0.5 \;\mathrm{mm}\\ I & = 2.48 \pm 0.04 \;\mathrm{A} \end{aligned}

Find the student's answer for the charge to mass ratio of the electron, with its uncertainty. Assume all uncertainties are independent and random.

**c)** A student finds the refractive index n of a piece of glass by measuring the critical angle в for light passing from the glass into air as $$\theta = 41 \pm 1^\circ.$$ The relation between these is known to be $$n = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}.$$ Find the student's answer for $$n$$ and its uncertainty.

desc: In radioactive decay, the number of isotopes present in a sample over time decreases exponentially: $$N(t) = N_0 (1/2)^{t/\tau}$$ where $$\tau$$ is the **half life** of the isotope. This formula is important in techniques such as radiocarbon dating, which allows scientists to…
statement:
In radioactive decay, the number of isotopes present in a sample over time decreases exponentially:

$$N(t) = N_0 (1/2)^{t/\tau}$$ where $$\tau$$ is the **half life** of the isotope.

This formula is important in techniques such as radiocarbon dating, which allows scientists to determine the age of a sample by assuming what the original isotope concentration was, measuring the current isotope concentration, and using the known half-life to determine the sample's age.

The origin of the formula is that each atom, independently, has a small chance $$p$$ to decay in any given second.

**a)** Find $$\tau$$ in terms of $$p.$$

**b)** A sample of $$N$$ atoms of some isotope triggers decay events at some rate $$r$$ (with dimensions of inverse time) over a time short compared to the half life. What is the half life in terms of $$r$$ and $$N?$$

statement:
In USAPhO and IPhO, there are two methods to find best fit lines, both of which are acceptable unless otherwise noted:

1) Simply draw the best-looking line you can through the data and estimating the slope by taking two points on that line. 2) Put the data into your calculator and have it calculate the **least squares linear regression**.

The calculator finds the best fit line using a method called "least squares linear regression". In this problem, we'll see how this method works.

No line can go through all the data points. There will always be some vertical distance between the line and a given data point. These vertical distances are called "residuals". In least squares linear regression, we find the line such that the sum of the residuals is as small as possible.

A physical analogy is to think of the best fit line as a straight massless rod. The data points can be thought of as pegs to which we attach springs of zero rest length. Then the other side of the spring is attached to the rod. The springs are constrained to be vertical. The length of each spring is the residual. The rod is allowed to rotate and move up and down until it finds equilibrium.

**a)** Explain why the equilibrium position of the rod described above is the least-squares linear regression line.

**b)** Write down the equations for force and torque balance on the rod. You will need to expression your answer in terms of sums over the $$x$$ and $$y$$ values $$x_i$$ and $$y_i$$ of the $$i$$th data point.

**c)** Solve the equations from part (b) to find the slope and y-intercept of the rod. Express your answer in terms of $$\bar{x}$$ and $$\bar{y},$$ the average of these values, and $$\mathrm{var}(x) = \dfrac{1}{N}\left(\sum_i x_i^2 \right) - \bar{x}^2.$$ and $$\mathrm{cov}(x,y) = \dfrac{1}{N}\left(\sum_i x_iy_i \right) - \bar{x}\bar{y}.$$ where $$N$$ is the number of data points.

The first of these is the variance of $$x.$$ The second is the covariance of $$x$$ and $$y.$$ (Note that the variance of $$x$$ is the covariance of $$x$$ with itself.)

Use this method to estimate the slope and error for the following data:

desc: This problem will introduce you to the Gaussian distribution. Contests often say to "assume Gaussian errors", which is not truly necessary for the error propagation formulas, but Gaussian distributions are very common in science. **a)** The Gaussian distribution is defined to be…
statement:
This problem will introduce you to the Gaussian distribution. Contests often say to "assume Gaussian errors", which is not truly necessary for the error propagation formulas, but Gaussian distributions are very common in science.

**a)** The Gaussian distribution is defined to be $$ p(x) = c \cdot \exp\left(\dfrac{-(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$

The meaning is that the probability for a measured value $$x$$ to be between $$x_1$$ and $$x_2$$ is $$P(x_1 < x < x_2) = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} p(x)\mathrm{d}x.$$

Find the constant $$c.$$ You may use the fact that $$\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}\mathrm{d}x = \sqrt{\pi}.$$

**b)** This part can be skipped, and simply shows one way to find the integral given at the end of part (a).

Consider the integral $$\iint_{x = -\infty, y=-\infty}^{x = \infty, y=\infty} e^{-x^2} e^{-y^2} \mathrm{d}x \mathrm{d}y.$$

Argue that this integral is the square of the one given at the end of part (a).

Evaluate the integral above by switching to polar coordinates, \begin{aligned} r^2 & = x^2 + y^2 \\ \tan\theta & = \frac{y}{x} \end{aligned}

You will need to make sure you integrate over the volume element in polar coordinates, which we discussed in the transcript of the class on friction.

From this, show \[\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}\mathrm{d}x = \sqrt{\pi}.\]

**c)** What is the mean of the Gaussian distribution?

The mean is defined by $$\langle x \rangle = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x p(x) \mathrm{d}x,$$ but you may be able to determine the mean without explicitly calculating the integral.

**d)** What is the standard deviation of the Gaussian distribution? This is defined by $$\sigma_x = \langle x^2 \rangle - \langle x \rangle^2.$$

And $$\langle x^2 \rangle = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x^2 p(x) \mathrm{d}x.$$

To evaluate this, you may want to consider $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha} \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-\alpha x^2}\mathrm{d}x.$$

**e)** Although some tricks can allow us to find the integral $$\int_{-\infty}^\infty p(x) \mathrm{d}x,$$ for other boundaries, the integral is evaluated numerically. The most-famous results are

\begin{aligned} \int_{-1}^1 e^{-x^2/2} \mathrm{d}x & \approx 0.683 \sqrt{2\pi}\\ \int_{-2}^2 e^{-x^2/2} \mathrm{d}x & \approx 0.955 \sqrt{2\pi}\\ \int_{-3}^3 e^{-x^2/2} \mathrm{d}x & \approx 0.997 \sqrt{2\pi} \end{aligned}

When sampling from a Gaussian distribution with mean $$\mu$$ and standard deviation $$\sigma,$$ what is the probability that the result will be between $$-\sigma$$ and $$2\sigma?$$

What is the probability that the result will be between $$\sigma$$ and $$3\sigma?$$

By "the height of the water", we mean the level of the surface of the water, relative to the level far away from the vortex.

The last part of this problem may help prepare you for some of the mathematics involved in Maxwell's equations, which we'll study next.

**d)** Read the definition of the (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circulation_(fluid_dynamics)).

Show that the circulation of the flow in a vortex is zero for a path that does not include the center of the vortex, and is equal to some constant for any path that does encircle the center. Another way to say this is that the **vorticity** is zero everywhere but the center, where it is a "delta function" (infinitely-high peak with finite area).

It's a strange fact that vortices have no vorticity! In fact, for an ideal fluid, this is always true - the circulation of any path is zero. This is called **Kelvin's Theorem**.

statement:
In this problem you will analyze two simplified models of blood flow in vessels.

Blood vessels are approximately cylindrical in shape, and it is known that for a steady, non turbulent flow of an incompressible fluid in a rigid cylinder, the difference in pressure of the fluid at the two ends of the cylinder is given by $$ \Delta P = \dfrac{8\ell \eta}{\pi r^4}Q,$$ where \begin{aligned} \ell & = \text{length of cylinder} \\ r & = \text{radius of cylinder} \\ \eta & = \text{viscosity of fluid} \\ Q & = \text{volumetric flow rate, i.e. volume that passes the cylinder cross section per unit time} \end{aligned}

This expression is often able to provide the correct order of magnitude for the pressure difference in a vessel, even without taking into account the pulsatile flow, the vessel's compressibility and irregular shape, and the fact that blood is not a simple fluid but a mixture of cells and plasma. Also, this expression has the same form as Ohm's law, with the volumetric flow rate being interpreted as a current, the difference in pressure as a voltage, and the factor $$R = \dfrac{8\ell \eta}{\pi r^4}$$ as a resistance.

Consider the symmetrical network of arterioles (small arteries), depicted in the figure below. This network delivers blood to the capillary bed of a tissue. In this network, at each bifurcation a vessel is divided in two. We will call this moving to a higher level of the network.

The vessels of higher levels are thinner and shorter than those of lower levels. Assume that the radii and lengths of vessels in two consecutive levels, $$i$$ and $$i+1,$$ are related by $$r_{i+1} = \dfrac{r_i}{2^{1/3}}.$$ and by $$\ell_{i+1} = \dfrac{\ell_i}{2^{1/3}}.$$

**a)** Obtain an expression for the volumetric flow rate, $$Q_i,$$ in a vessel at any level $$i$$ as a function of the total number of levels $$N,$$ the viscosity $$\eta,$$ the radius $$r_0$$ and length $$\ell_0$$ of the first vessel, and the difference $$\Delta P = P_0 - P_{\mathrm{cap}}$$ between the pressure at the arteriole at level 0, $$P_0,$$ and the pressure at the capillary bed, $$P_{\mathrm{cap}}.$$

**b)** Calculate the numerical value of the volumetric flow rate $$Q_0$$ of the arteriole at level 0, if its radius is $$6.0 \times 10^{-5} \;\mathrm{m}$$ and its length is $$2.0 \times 10^{-3} \;\mathrm{m}.$$ Assume that the pressure at the arteriole inlet is $$7.3 \times 10^3 \;\mathrm{Pa}$$ and the vessel network has $$N = 6$$ levels linking this arteriole to the capillary bed at the pressure $$4.0 \times 10^3 \;\mathrm{Pa}.$$ Assume that the blood viscosity is $$\eta = 3.5 \times 10^{-3} \;\mathrm{kg m^{-1} s^{-1}}.$$ Express your result in $$\mathrm{ml/h}.$$

statement:
This problem extends the previous one, making an analogy between fluid flow and an LRC circuit. We'll study RLC circuits in class 10. You may want to work this problem now as a preview of that material, or wait and return to this material in several weeks.

**A blood vessel as an RLC circuit**

The approximation of rigid cylindrical vessels falls short for several reasons. It is particularly important to include the time dependent flow and to take into account the change in vessel diameter that occurs when the pressure varies during a blood pumping cycle done by the heart. Also, it is observed that in the larger vessels the blood pressure varies significantly during a cycle, while in the smaller vessels the amplitude of the oscillations in pressure is much smaller, and the flow is almost time independent.

When the pressure increases in a single elastic vessel, there will be an increase in its diameter, thus permitting it to store more fluid in the vessel, and to deliver it when the pressure drops. For this reason, the elastic behaviour of the vessel can be simulated by adding a capacitor to our initial description. Moreover, when taking into account the time dependent blood flow rate, one has to consider the inertia of the fluid, proportional to its density $$\rho = 1.05\times 10^3 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$ This inertia can be described by an inductance in our model. In the figure below we represent the equivalent circuit for a single vessel in this model. The equivalent capacitance and inductance are given by $$C = \dfrac{3\ell \pi r^3}{2Eh}.$$ $$L = \dfrac{9\ell \rho}{4\pi r^2}$$ respectively, where $$h$$ is the width of the vessel wall and $$E$$ is the artery Young's modulus, a coefficient that describes the alteration in size of the vessel tissue when a force is applied. The Young's modulus has units of pressure and is on the order of $$E = 0.06\;\mathrm{MPa}$$ for arterioles.

**c)** Obtain, in the stationary regime, the pressure amplitude at the vessel outlet, $$P_{\mathrm{out}},$$ as a function of the pressure amplitude at the inlet, $$P_{\mathrm{in}},$$ the equivalent resistance, $$R,$$ inductance, $$L,$$ and capacitance $$C$$ for a flow with angular frequency $$\omega.$$ Establish the condition between $$\eta, \rho, E, h, r,$$ and $$\ell$$ so that, for low frequencies, the pressure oscillation amplitude at the outlet is smaller than that of $$P_{\mathrm{in}}.$$

**d)** For the vessel network in part (b) of the previous problem, estimate the maximum arteriole wall thickness $$h$$ so that the condition established in (c) is satisfied. (Assume that $$h$$ is the same at all levels.)

This problem involves electric polarizability, which we will cover in future weeks, in addition to fluid dynamics. The relevant definition is given in the problem. You may wish to work the prior problem about a vortex first first, and recall its discussion of Kelvin's theorem, and to review the continuity equation and its relation to Gauss' law. When a body moves in liquid, the motion of the body puts the liquid into motion, too. The motion of liquid contributes to the total kinetic energy of the system, and hence, leads to an increased __effective mass__ of the body. The difference of the effective mass and the actual mass of the body is referred to as the added mass. The added mass depends on the size and shape of the body.

Consider a certain metallic body of volume $$V$$ and polarizability $$\alpha$$ along its symmetry axis $$x$$ (i.e. homogeneous externally applied electric field $$\vec{E}$$ induces total dipole moment $$\vec{p} = \alpha \vec{E}$$ on this body). statement:
In the late 19th century the American student Edwin Hall was given the problem of observing the effect of a magnetic field on electrons traveling in a conductor. He was successful, and measured what is now known as the __Hall Effect__.

The figure below illustrates Hall's experiment conceptually.

A current is passed through a strip of gold leaf and the current carriers (usually electrons) pass through the gold leaf. The current passes through the gold leaf in the direction shown.

There is a magnetic field as shown as well. The magnetic field acts on the moving current carriers and these carriers are pulled to the left.

One thin edge of the gold leaf becomes positively-charged (colored pink in the drawing), relative to the other side. This results in a potential difference across the gold leaf in the direction perpendicular to the current and the magnetic field. This potential difference is called the __Hall voltage__.

**d)** The highest field available is $$0.1 \;\mathrm{T}.$$ The width of the gold leaf is $$40 \;\mathrm{mm},$$ the thickness is $$10 \;\mathrm{mm},$$ and the current is $$200 \;\mathrm{mA}.$$ What is the drift velocity of the free electrons? statement:
This problem describes the phenomenon of __magnetoresistance__, which is used, for example, to create hard disk read/write heads.

Magnetic properties of electrons are intrinsically related to their spin. In ferromagnetic materials, unpaired electron spins line up with each other within regions called domains. Within domains the magnetic field is therefore intense, though domains will generally be randomly orientated with respect to one another so that a bulk sample will usually be unmagnetized. However, an externally applied magnetic field can cause the magnetic domains to line up with each other; the material is said to be magnetized.

Electrons, although point particles, behave as if they were spinning and act like tiny magnets. Electrons in a ferromagnet whose spins are oriented in the direction of (parallel), or opposite to (antiparallel), the internal magnetization carry independent currents, leading to the material behaving as if it has different resistivities $$\rho_p$$ and $$\rho_a$$ for each of the two current components.

Two ferromagnetic layers with identical dimensions (length $$\ell,$$ cross-sectional area $$A)$$ but opposite magnetization are placed next to each other in parallel with a cell of e.m.f. $$\varepsilon$$ and internal resistance $$r.$$

The resistance of the rest of the external circuit is modeled by a resistance $$R$$ in series with the ferromagnetic layers.

**a)** Draw a diagram of the circuit described above.

**b)** Find the total resistance of the circuit.

**c)** An external magnetic field is now applied to the ferromagnetic layers, causing their magnetization to line up. Draw a new circuit diagram and find the total resistance in this case.

**d)** The current component parallel flows much more easily than that antiparallel, meaning that $$\rho_p \ll \rho_a.$$ Find an expression for the change in current between the two situations before and after the external field is applied.

**e)** For fixed resistances (and fixed resistivities $$\rho_p \ll \rho_a,)$$ under what conditions is the change in current maximized?

statement:
Magnetic fields are everywhere around us. Some typical magnetic $$B$$-field values:

Earth's magnetic field: $$25 - 60 \;\mathrm{\mu T}.$$ sunspots: $$0.3 \;\mathrm{T}.$$ strong permanent magnets: $$\sim 1\;\mathrm{T}.$$ continuously-maintained fields in laboratory: up to $$45 \;\mathrm{T}.$$ neutron stars and magnetars: up to $$10^{11}\;\mathrm{T}.$$

The energy density of a magnetic field is $$w = B^2 \dfrac{1}{2\mu \mu_0},$$ where $$\mu_0 \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-6} \;\mathrm{N/A^2}$$ is the vacuum permeability, and $$\mu$$ the relative permeability of the medium.

Systems try to move toward lower-energy states, so ferromagnetic materials, which have $$\mu \gg 1,$$ are pulled towards regions with strong magnetic fields. Diamagnetic materials have $$\mu < 1$$ and are pushed out from magnetic fields. For diamagnetic materials, the magnetic susceptibility $$\chi = \mu - 1$$ is small, $$|\chi| \ll 1,$$ and so the effect is small unless the field is strong. Water is diamagnetic with $$\chi = -9 \times 10^{-6}$$ and animals are mostly made of water. So, a frog can levitate in a magnetic field if the field is strong enough, as shown below.

**a)** Let the frog height, $$h_f,$$ be not more than $$h_0 = 10 \;\mathrm{mm},$$ and let us assume that the squared magnetic field depends linearly on height $$z$$ as shown below.

Assume that the frog is made entirely of water with density $$\rho = 1000 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$ Free fall acceleration is $$g = 9.8 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

hint:

for $$|\chi| \ll 1,$$ we can write $$w \approx B^2 \dfrac{1-\chi}{2\mu_0}.$$ This means the energy density associated with the presence of water is $$\Delta w = B^2 \dfrac{1-\chi}{2\mu_0} - B^2 \dfrac{1}{2\mu_0} = -B^2 \dfrac{\chi}{2\mu_0}.$$

desc: All particles have a fundamental property called __spin__. Spin is an intrinsic form of angular momentum. A full treatment of spin requires quantum mechanics, but we can still study spin using classical electromagnetism. In this problem, we investigate the influence of a…
statement:
All particles have a fundamental property called __spin__. Spin is an intrinsic form of angular momentum. A full treatment of spin requires quantum mechanics, but we can still study spin using classical electromagnetism. In this problem, we investigate the influence of a magnetic field on spin using classical physics.

The torque on a spin is given by $$\vec{\tau} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{L}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \vec{\mu}\times \vec{B}.$$

In this case, the angular momentum $$\vec{L}$$ represents the "instrinsic" spin of the particles, $$\vec{\mu}$$ is the magnetic moment of the particles, and $$\vec{B}$$ is the magnetic field. The spin of a particle is associated with a magnetic moment via the equation $$\vec{\mu} = -\gamma \vec{L}$$ where $$\gamma$$ is the __gyromagnetic ratio__.

**a)** Prove that the magnitude of magnetic moment $$\mu$$ is always constant under the influence of a magnetic field $$\vec{B}.$$ For the special case of a constant magnetic field, also show that the angle between $$\vec{\mu}$$ and $$\vec{B}$$ is constant.

**b)** A uniform magnetic field $$\vec{B}$$ exists and it makes an angle $$\phi$$ with a particle's magnetic moment $$\vec{\mu}.$$ Due to the torque by the magnetic field, the magnetic moment $$\vec{\mu}$$ rotates around the field $$\vec{B},$$ which is also known as Larmor precession. Determine the Larmor precession frequency $$\omega_0$$ of the magnetic moment with respect to $$\vec{B} = B_0 \hat{k}.$$

--------------

Next, we choose a rotating frame $$S'$$ as our frame of reference. The rotating frame $$S' = (x',y',z')$$ rotates with an angular velocity $$\omega \hat{k}$$ as seen by an observer in the laboratory frame $$S = (x,y,z).$$ The axes $$x',y',z'$$ intersect with $$x,y,z$$ at time $$t = 0.$$ Any vector $$\vec{A} = A_x \hat{i} + A_y \hat{j} + A_z \hat{k}$$ in a lab frame can be written as $$\vec{A} = A_x' \hat{i}' + A_y' \hat{j}' + A_z' \hat{k}'$$ in the rotating frame $$S'.$$ The time derivative of the vector becomes

$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{A}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \left( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}A_x'}{\mathrm{d}t} \hat{i}' + \dfrac{\mathrm{d}A_y'}{\mathrm{d}t} \hat{j}' + \dfrac{\mathrm{d}A_z'}{\mathrm{d}t}\hat{k}' \right) + \left(A_x' \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\hat{i}'}{\mathrm{d}t} + A_y' \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\hat{j}'}{\mathrm{d}t} + A_z' \dfrac{\mathrm{d}k'}{\mathrm{d}t}\right).$$

$$\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{A}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)_{\mathrm{lab}} = \left( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{A}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)_{\mathrm{rot}} + \left(\omega \hat{k} \times \vec{A}\right),$$

where $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{A}}{\mathrm{d}t}_{\mathrm{lab}}$$ is the time derivative of the vector $$\vec{A}$$ seen by an observer in the lab frame, and $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{A}}{\mathrm{d}t}_{\mathrm{rot}}$$ is the time derivative seen by an observer in the rotating frame. For all the following problems, the answers are referred to the rotating frame $$S'.$$

**c)** Show that the time evolution of the magnetic moment follows the equation $$\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{\mu}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)_{\mathrm{rot}} = -\gamma \vec{\mu}\times \vec{B}_{\mathrm{eff}},$$ where $$\vec{B}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \vec{B} - \dfrac{\omega}{\gamma} \hat{k}'$$ is the effective magnetic field.

**d)** For $$\vec{B} = B_0 \hat{k},$$ what is the new precession frequency $$\Delta$$ in terms of $$\omega_0$$ and $$\omega?$$

**e)** Now, let us consider the case of a time-varying magnetic field. Besides a constant magnetic field, we also apply a rotating magnetic field $$\vec{b}(t) = b(\cos \omega t \hat{i} + \sin \omega t \hat{j}),$$ so $$\vec{B} = B_0 \hat{k} + \vec{b}(t).$$

Show that the new Larmor precession frequency of the magnetic moment is $$\Omega = \gamma \sqrt{\left(B_0 - \dfrac{\omega}{\gamma}\right)^2 + b^2}.$$

**f)** Instead of applying the field $$\vec{b}(t) = b(\cos \omega t \hat{i} + \sin \omega t \hat{j}),$$ now we apply $$\vec{b}(t) = b(\cos \omega \hat{i} - \sin \omega t \hat{j}.$$ What is the effective magnetic field $$\vec{B}_{\mathrm{eff}}$$ for this case (in terms of the unit vectors $$\hat{i}', \hat{j}', \hat{k}')?$$ What is its time average, $$\overline{\vec{B}}_{\mathrm{eff}}?$$

desc: This problem continues the previous one on spin. For an ensemble of $$N$$ particles under the influence of a large magnetic field, the spin can have two quantum states: "up" and "down". Consequently, the total population of spin up $$N_{\uparrow}$$ and down $$N_{\downarrow}$$…
statement:
This problem continues the previous one on spin.

For an ensemble of $$N$$ particles under the influence of a large magnetic field, the spin can have two quantum states: "up" and "down". Consequently, the total population of spin up $$N_{\uparrow}$$ and down $$N_{\downarrow}$$ obeys the equation $$N_{\uparrow} + N_{\downarrow} = N.$$

The difference of spin up population and spin down population yields the macroscopic magnetization along the $$z$$ axis: $$ M = (N_{\uparrow} - N_{\downarrow}) \mu = N\mu_z.$$

In a real experiment, two magnetic field are usually applied, a large bias field $$B_0 \hat{k}$$ and an oscillating field with amplitude $$2b$$ perpendicular to the bias field $$(b \ll B_0).$$ Initially, only the large bias is applied, causing all the particles to lie in the spin up states ($$\vec{\mu}$$ is oriented in the $$z$$ direction at $$t=0).$$ Then, the oscillating field is turned on, where its frequency $$\omega$$ is chosen to be in resonance with the Larmor precession frequency $$\omega_0,$$ i.e. $$\omega = \omega_0.$$ In other words, the total field after time $$t=0$$ is given by $$\vec{B}(t) = B_0 \hat{k} + 2b \cos \omega_0 t \hat{i}.$$

**g)** In the totating frame $$S',$$ show that the effective field can be approximated by $$B_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx b \hat{i},$$ which is commonly known as the __rotating wave approximation__. What is the precession frequency $$\Omega$$ in frame $$S'?$$

**h)** Determine the angle $$\alpha$$ that $$\vec{\mu}$$ makes with $$\vec{B}_{\mathrm{eff}}.$$ Also, prove that the magnetization varies with time as $$M(t) = N \mu(\cos \Omega t).$$

**i)** Under the application of the magnetic field described above, determine the fractional population of each spin up $$P_{\uparrow} = N_{\uparrow}/N$$ and spin down $$P_{\downarrow} = N_{\downarrow}/N$$ as a function of time. Plot $$P_{\uparrow}(t)$$ and $$P_{\downarrow}(t)$$ on the same graph vs time $$t.$$ The alternating spin up and spin down population as a function of time is called __Rabi oscillation__.

statement:
Mechanical and electrical processes are sometimes strongly coupled. Very important examples are systems containing piezoelectric materials, e.g. quartz resonators. Here we investigate a somewhat-simpler situation.

There are two metal plates with area $$S$$ and mass $$m.$$ One plate is situated atop of the other one. Plates are connected to each other with springs, whose total spring constant is $$k.$$ The springs are made of an insulator. The lower plate is mounted on a steady base. The equilibrium distance between the plates is $$X_0.$$

**a)** Let us assume that there is a small vertical shift $$x$$ of the upper plate from its equilibrium position. Derive the acceleration $$\ddot{x}$$ of $$x$$ in terms of the system parameters. What is the angular frequency $$\omega_0$$ of the small vertical oscillations of the upper plate?

**b)** The plates are now connected to a constant high voltage source, so that they form a capacitor. Electrostatic forces between the plates cause an additional shift of the upper plate. The equilibrium distance between the plates is now $$X_1.$$ Derive expressions of the electrical attractive force $$F_e$$ and voltage applied to the plates $$U$$ in terms of $$X_0, X_1, S, m$$ and $$k.$$

**c)** The system is set to oscillate again, keeping the voltage $$U$$ constant. Let $$x$$ stand still for the shift from the equilibrium position. Derive an expression for the acceleration $$\ddot{x}$$ of $$x$$ in terms of $$X_0, X_1, S, m, k,$$ and $$x.$$ What is the angular frequency $$\omega_1$$ of the upper plate's small vertical oscillations?

**a)** An AC power line cable transmits electrical power using a sinusoidal waveform with frequency $$60 \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ The load receives an RMS voltage of $$500 \;\mathrm{kV}$$ and requires $$1000 \;\mathrm{MW}$$ of average power. For this problem, consider only the cable carrying current in one of the two directions, and ignore effects due to capacitance or inductance between the cable and with the ground.

**b)** The cable has diameter $$3 \;\mathrm{cm},$$ is $$500 \;\mathrm{km}$$ long, and is made of aluminum with resistivity $$2.8 \times 10^{-8} \;\mathrm{\Omega \cdot m}.$$ How much power is lost in the wire?

**c)** A local rancher thinks he might be able to extract electrical power from the cable using electromagnetic induction. the rancher constructs a rectangular loop of length $$a$$ and width $$b < a,$$ consisting of $$N$$ turns of wire. One edge of the loop is to be placed on the ground; the wire is straight and runs parallel to the ground at a height $$h$$ much less than the length of the wire. statement:
**note:** This problem provides a review of geometric optics and Fermat's principle of least time, but not interference and diffraction.

In 1838, Samuel Birley Rowbotham placed a series of poles of known height in the Old Bedford River in England. Rowbotham found that light rays traveled at a constant distance above the surface of the lake over the course of six miles, and concluded that the Earth is flat.

**a)** Qualitatively explain why light may travel a long distance across the surface of the Earth remaining at approximately the same elevation, when traveling in a straight line would result in gaining elevation due to the Earth curving away underneath the path of the light.

**b)** Estimate the temperature gradient in air, in degrees $$K$$ per meter, needed for light to follow a path with the same radius of curvature as Earth. You can take the index of refraction of air to be $$1.0003$$ at one atmosphere and $$300\;\mathrm{K},$$ and to vary linearly with the density of air. You may assume that difference in the density of air due to temperature are much larger than those due to differences in pressure. The radius of Earth is $$R \approx 6.4 \times 10^6 \;\mathrm{m}.$$

When driving on a hot road, one often sees a mirage.

We will assume you are driving on a perfectly flat road.

**c)** Suppose your eye is at point $$E.$$ There is some point $$B$$ which is the furthest point along the road at which light from the road still reaches your eye.

Suppose the index of refraction at the air just above the road is $$n_B.$$ What is the index of refraction of the air at your eye, $$n_E?$$ Give your answer in terms of the the angle $$\theta_E$$ that light makes with the vertical as it enters your eye.

**d)** Suppose that, due to the atmosphere, the speed of light decreases linearly with height above the road. What is the trajectory of a light ray?

Near the slit, this just produces a beam which is less intense by a factor of two on the edges. Far away, however, the diffraction pattern is quite different from that of the single slit. **note** Portions of this problem concern diffraction, while other portions preview concepts of electromagnetic radiation we will study in more detail next class.

It has been proposed that tiny probes could be sent to other stars by accelerating them away from Earth using a powerful laser.

**a)** To push the probe hard enough for it to reach other solar systems will require a large laser focused on the sail of a small probe. One way of focusing the laser is to make use of existing optics by using a telescope in reverse. Given a telescope of diameter $$D$$ emitting a laser beam of wavelength $$\lambda$$ and a probe sail of diameter $$d,$$ what is the distance $$R$$ the probe can get before less the 90% of the light hits the sail? How far is this for a sail of size $$1 \;\mathrm{m},$$ a telescope diameter of $$10 \;\mathrm{m},$$ and a laser wavelength of $$600 \;\mathrm{nm}?$$ (You may give an estimate; a precise calculation is not needed.)

**b)** Assume that when the monochromatic laser light hits the sail of the probe at right angles it has power $$W.$$ What is the force $$F$$ exerted on a black (perfectly absorbing) sail and a silvered (perfectly reflective) sail?

**c)** Using your previous expression, find the time it would take a probe of mass $$m$$ to travel a distance $$L.$$ For simplification, you may assume that the probe feels the full force of the laser beam up to a distance $$R,$$ and nothing after that, and that it has a perfectly reflective sail. The proposal calls for the probe to have mass $$10^{-3} \;\mathrm{kg},$$ the laser power to be $$100 \;\mathrm{GW},$$ and for the probe to go to Alpha Centauri, which is $$4.2$$ light years away. Using the optics described in the first part, how long will this take?

**d)** One way of reducing this time considerably is to increase $$R$$ by using a different optical set up. Rather than using one telescope, several telescopes could on different bits of land could be used together in order to create an interference pattern. What is the maximum possible effective diameter of such a setup? What would be the travel time to Alpha Centauri under this setup? (Only an approximate answer is desired.)

Monochromatic light can be focused into a point using a holographic lens (better known as a __Fresnel zone plate__). This is a thin film which has a system of opaque and transparent concentric rings: the opaque rings obstruct those light waves which would arrive at the focus in the opposite phase (as compared with the light from the transparent rings). **b)** Let us consider also a glass lens of the same focal length $$f$$ and diameter $$d$$, such that a parallel incident beam is collected perfectly into the focus. (The lens has aspherical surfaces.) What is the minimal possible thickness of such a lens if the coefficient of refraction of the glass is $$n = 1.5?$$

**c)** If a short light pulse falls onto a lens, the behavior of the holographic lens is very different from that of the glass lens. Indeed, if we ignore the dispersion of the glass (the dependence of $$n$$ on the wavelength,) the pulse duration at the focus of the glass lens is the same as that of the incident beam. Meanwhile, in the case of a short pulse ($$\tau = 3\times 10^{-14} \;\mathrm{s}),$$ the pulse durations at the focus of the holographic lens become significantly dilated. Sketch qualitatively the light intensity $$I$$ at the focus of the holographic lens as a function of time. statement:
In the handout, we saw that the dispersion relation for gravity-driven water waves in deep water is $$\omega_{\rm deep \, water} = \sqrt{gk}.$$ In this problem, we look at what happens when the water is not deep compared to $$\dfrac{1}{k}.$$

**a)** Explain why, in this case, we cannot determine the dispersion relationship via dimensional analysis alone.

**b)** The basic theory of these waves, assuming the amplitude of the waves is small compared to $$h,$$ states that $$\omega^2 = gk {\rm tanh}(kh)$$ where $$h$$ is the depth of the water. Show that this recovers the deep water dispersion relation in the appropriate limit.

**c)** In the limit of shallow water, how does the speed of a wave depend on its wavelength?

**d)** Suppose the amplitude of the wave is not small compared to $$h.$$ Which moves faster - the crest of a wave or the trough?

**e)** Qualitatively explain why waves break as they approach the shore of the ocean.

desc: In this problem, we investigate the group velocity, $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}k}$$ for waves in a dispersive medium (one in which the phase velocity $$\dfrac{\omega}{k}$$ depends on $$\omega$$.) **a)** Briefly explain why a simple harmonic wave does not transmit…
statement:
In this problem, we investigate the group velocity, $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}k}$$ for waves in a dispersive medium (one in which the phase velocity $$\dfrac{\omega}{k}$$ depends on $$\omega$$.)

**a)** Briefly explain why a simple harmonic wave does not transmit information from place to place. For example, explain why a radio station cannot truly broadcast on a single frequency.

**b)** Instead, for a wave to transmit information, there will need to be at least two frequencies involved. We will study the simplest case. Imagine a wave traveling through some medium along the $$x$$ axis. At $$x = 0,$$ the displacement is $$\Psi = A \cos \omega_1 t + A \cos\omega_2 t$$

This wave can be written $$\Psi(0,t) = 2A \cos \omega_{\rm mod}t \cos \omega_{\rm av} t. $$

Find $$\omega_{\rm mod}$$ and $$\omega_{\rm av}.$$

**c)** Suppose $$|\omega_1 - \omega_2| \ll \omega_1.$$ How do $$\omega_{\rm mod}$$ and $$\omega_{\rm av}$$ compare?

Explain why this sort of wave is called an __amplitude-modulated__ wave. (Like AM radio.)

**d)** Find $$\Psi(x,t)$$ using $$k_1$$ and $$k_2,$$ the wavenumbers associated with $$\omega_1$$ and $$\omega_2.$$ Do not assume a non-dispersive wave. Rewrite the result in terms of $$\omega_{\rm mod}, \omega_{\rm av}, k_{\rm mod},$$ and $$k_{\rm av}.$$ Give the definitions of $$k_{\rm mod}$$ and $$k_{\rm av}.$$ Draw a sketch of the wave.

**e)** Your sketch from part (d) should show \emph{modulations}, places where the amplitude of the wave is large and places where the amplitude is small. What is the speed of propagation of the modulations? Write your answer first in terms of $$\omega_{\rm mod}$$ and $$k_{\rm mod},$$ then in terms of $$\omega_1, \omega_2, k_1,$$ and $$k_2.$$

**f)** Again assuming $$|\omega_1 - \omega_2|$$ is small, rewrite your result, to first order, as a derivative.

**g)** Reviewing your work, explain the interpretation of the group velocity.

desc: A theory for the origin of the index of refraction of electromagnetic waves through a dilute gas gives the result $$n^2 = 1 + N\alpha$$ where $$n$$ is the index of refraction, $$N$$ is the number density of the atoms (number of atoms per unit volume), and $$\alpha$$ is the…
statement:
A theory for the origin of the index of refraction of electromagnetic waves through a dilute gas gives the result $$n^2 = 1 + N\alpha$$ where $$n$$ is the index of refraction, $$N$$ is the number density of the atoms (number of atoms per unit volume), and $$\alpha$$ is the atomic polarizability, defined by $$\vec{p} = \epsilon_0 \alpha \vec{E}$$ where $$\vec{p}$$ is the electric dipole moment of an individual atom and $$\vec{E}$$ is an applied electric field.

In this problem, we will not examine the full theory of the origin of the index of refraction, but will attempt to understand some of the results.

**a)** Given the result above, find the dispersion relation for the material.

**b)** The above result is derived from a model in which an electron is considered a tiny charged ball with mass $$m$$ and charge $$e$$ attached to the immovable nucleus via a spring with some spring constant $$\kappa.$$ (We use $$\kappa$$ for the spring constant so that $$k$$ is reserved for the wavenumber.)The forces on the electron are those from the spring, a damping force $$F_d = m\gamma \dot{x}$$ for some coefficient $$\gamma$$ (where $$x$$ is the displacement of the electron from equilibrium), and an electric force from the passing electromagnetic wave.

For what frequency of light do you expect the largest polarizability of the atom?

**c)** Estimate this frequency as a function of $$h, e, \epsilon_0,$$ and $$m,$$ where $$h$$ is Planck's constant, $$h \approx 6.6\times 10^{-34} \;\mathrm{J\cdot s}.$$ Find the resonant frequency to order of magnitude. What sort of electromagnetic wave is this? Is the index of refraction particularly low or particularly high at this frequency? For visible light, is the index of refraction increasing or decreasing with wavelength?

**d)** Based on this model, give a qualitative explanation of why the index of refraction varies depending on wavelength. That is, explain the origin of dispersion.

**e)** In such a model, what happens to the amplitude of an electromagnetic wave as it travels through a thick pane of glass? How do you know?

**d)** Show that the wave can obey Maxwell's equations. In order to obey Maxwell's equation, what must be $$\phi, \dfrac{E_0}{B_0},$$ and $$\dfrac{\omega}{k}?$$

statement:
We have studied electromagnetic waves in various contexts, but so far they have all be plane waves.

Another important case is a spherical wave. This is a wave in which all the wavefronts are spheres.

Try to find a solution to the wave equation in three dimensions representing a spherical wave.

The wave equation in three dimensions is $$ \dfrac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial y^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial z^2} = \dfrac{1}{c^2} \dfrac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial t^2}.$$

In spherical coordinates, assuming the wave has no dependence on $$\theta$$ or $$\phi,$$ the equation becomes $$ \dfrac{1}{r^2} \dfrac{\partial}{\partial r} \left( r^2 \dfrac{\partial \Psi}{\partial r}\right) = \dfrac{1}{c^2} \dfrac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial t^2}.$$

You may want to guess at the form of the solution on physical grounds, then verify that the solution is correct.

desc: This problem continues a problem on interference from class 11. Consider an opaque barrier in the $$x-y$$ plane at $$z = 0,$$ with a single slit along the $$x$$ axis of width $$2a,$$ but with regions on either side of the slit each with width $$2a$$ which are partially…
statement:
This problem continues a problem on interference from class 11.

Consider an opaque barrier in the $$x-y$$ plane at $$z = 0,$$ with a single slit along the $$x$$ axis of width $$2a,$$ but with regions on either side of the slit each with width $$2a$$ which are partially transparent, designed to reduce the intensity by a factor of $$2.$$ When this barrier is illuminated by a plane wave in the $$z$$ direction, the amplitude of the oscillating field at $$z = 0$$ is $$f(x,y)e^{i\omega t}$$ for \begin{aligned} f(x,y) & = 1 ;& |y| < a \\ f(x,y) & = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} ;& a < |y| < 3a \\ f(x,y) & = 0 ; & 3a < |y| \end{aligned}

Near the slit, this just produces a beam which is less intense by a factor of two on the edges. Far away, however, the diffraction pattern is quite different from that of the single slit. At a fixed large distance $$R = \sqrt{y^2 + z^2}$$ away from the slit, the intensity as a function of $$\xi = k_y a = \dfrac{\omega y a}{cR}$$ is shown in the figure below for positive $$\xi.$$

The value of the peak of $$\xi = 0$$ is normalized to $$1,$$ but has been suppressed in the graph to show the details of the secondary maxima.

**a)** (done in week 11, re-presented as a reminder) Find the smallest positive value of $$\xi$$ for which the intensity vanishes.

**b)** (done in week 11, re-presented as a reminder) Find the ratio of the intensity at $$\xi = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$$ to that at $$\xi = 0.$$

**c)** (new for this week) So far, we have not mentioned the polarization of the light, assuming that it is irrelevant. In fact, we get the pattern shown above for any polarization, so long as the shading doesn't affect the polarization (and $$\xi$$ is small). However, if the light is initially polarized in the direction $$45^\circ$$ from the $$x$$ axis, we could reduce the intensity by two by passing it through a perfect polarizer aligned with the $$y$$ axis. Suppose that our slit between $$-a$$ and $$a$$ is completely empty, but between $$-3a$$ and $$-a$$ and between $$a$$ and $$3a,$$ we put such a polarizer. Now, as before, the beam close to the slit just has the intensity on the edges reduced by a factor of $$2.$$ However, the diffraction pattern is quite different. As a function of $$\xi,$$ the intensity at large fixed $$R$$ is $$\propto \dfrac{1}{10} \left[ \left( \dfrac{\sin 3\xi}{\xi}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\sin \xi}{\xi}\right)^2 \right],$$ which looks nothing like the pattern above. Explain the difference.
