At the 2004 International Physics Olympiad in Korea, a demonstration showed how a table tennis ball could make a hole in ceramic plates. Photos from the demonstration are below.

The ceramic plates were placed between two glass tubes. The tubes were then evacuated so that there was a vacuum on each side of the plates. Suddenly, the tube was opened on the side of the ball adjacent to the end of the tube, as shown in figure 2.1. The atmospheric pressure on that side shot the ball into the plates, making a hole in the plates. We can assume that the ball made an airtight fit with the tube, and neglect any friction between the ball and the tube.

**a)** Find the maximum speed at which the ball could conceivably hit the plates, assuming the temperature in the air was $$300 \;\mathrm{K}$$ and that air is made of nitrogen molecules.

**b)** The ball has a mass of $$0.01 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ Calculate its maximum conceivable kinetic energy.

**c)** Consider a cubic box of side length $$L$$ and volume $$V$$ containing $$n$$ molecules, each of mass $$m,$$ and all moving in random directions at constant speed $$v.$$ All collisions are assumed to be perfectly elastic, and the total volume of the molecules is much less than $$V.$$

What is the change in momentum when a molecule, moving in an arbitrary direction, hits a face of the box with speed $$u$$ normal to the face of the box?

**d)** Calculate the average time it takes this molecule to traverse the box.

**e)** Using the results from (c) and (d), find the pressure in the box as a function of $$V, n, m,$$ and $$v.$$

Suppose we follow an individual molecule in a gas. It travels some distance, then has a collision with another molecule, changing its direction of motion. **a)** Via dimensional analysis and some intuition, estimate $$\lambda$$ for a dilute gas of hard spheres with radius $$r$$ and number density $$n.$$

**b)** A surprising experimental result is that the viscosity of a gas does not depend on its density. Explain how this can be the case, given that viscosity does depend linearly on both number density and mean free path.

**c)** Suppose the mean free path in some gas is $$\lambda.$$ Suppose we are watching a molecule, at it has already traveled a distance $$\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$$ without any collisions. What is the mean distance it will travel before its next collision?

statement:
When we study quantum mechanics, we will use the Bohr model to discover that the energy levels of a hydrogen atom obey $$E_n = -\dfrac{E_0}{n^2},$$ where $$E_0 \approx 13.6 \;\mathrm{eV}$$ is the ionization energy of the hydrogen atom and $$n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots.$$

The number of different states for an electron with energy $$E_n$$ is $$2n^2.$$ So there are two different ground states ($$n=1$$) for the electron (because it is in the ground state, but its spin can be either up or down). Then there are 8 different states all with the energy $$E_2.$$ If you have studied chemistry, you know these as the $$2s$$ and $$2p$$ states (which have the same energy for a hydrogen atom). There are 18 states with energy $$E_3,$$ etc.

Suppose a hydrogen atom is in thermal contact with a reservoir of temperature $$T = 300 \;\mathrm{K},$$ about room temperature.

**a)** Estimate the probability that the Hydrogen atom is not at its ground state energy. For this estimate, assume that the only two possible states are the ground state and the first excited state; ignore the higher-$$n$$ states on the ground that when $$n$$ is very large, the mathematical solution is no longer reasonable; the orbital radius would also be very large, and small influences from surroundings would ionize the atom.

**b)** Find the temperature at which the electron electron is equally likely to have energy $$E_1$$ or $$E_2.$$

**c)** We might expect hydrogen atoms to begin ionizing at a temperature where $$k_b T \approx E_0,$$ but in fact significant ionization occurs at much lower temperatures, especially if the hydrogen is in a gas or plasma of very low density. Briefly explain why.

Estimate the initial acceleration $$a_0$$ and maximal speed $$v_{\rm max}$$ of the disk during its subsequent motion.

Assume the hat capacity of the disk to be on the order of $$N k_B,$$ where $$N$$ is the number of atoms in it, and $$k_B$$ is the Boltzmann constant. Also assume that the molar mass of the gas and disk's materials are the same. The mean free path length of the gas molecules is much larger than the size of the disk. name: This problem introduces the __partition function__, a useful tool for calculations…
desc: This problem introduces the __partition function__, a useful tool for calculations involving the Boltzmann factor and degeneracy of energy levels. **a)** Suppose that a system is in thermal contact with a reservoir at temperature $$T,$$ so that the probability of the system…
statement:
This problem introduces the __partition function__, a useful tool for calculations involving the Boltzmann factor and degeneracy of energy levels.

**a)** Suppose that a system is in thermal contact with a reservoir at temperature $$T,$$ so that the probability of the system being in any given state of energy $$E_i$$ is proportional to $$e^{-E_i/k_B T}.$$

That is, the probability to be in state $$i$$ is $$P_i = \dfrac{1}{Z} e^{-E_i/k_B T}$$ for some $$Z.$$

Write $$Z$$ as a sum over $$i$$.

**b)** $$Z$$ is called the __partition function__. For any given system, $$Z$$ is a function of $$T.$$

Often, it is useful to define $$\beta = \dfrac{1}{k_B T},$$ in which case $$Z$$ is a function of $$\beta.$$

Show that the mean energy of the system is given by $$ \langle E\rangle = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \beta} \ln Z.$$

**c)** In physics, it shouldn't matter where we set the zero of potential energy. Suppose we add some energy $$E_0$$ to all the energy levels of a system. Show that the probabilities of individual energy levels do not change according to our formalism, and find the new mean energy.

**d)** It is sometimes useful to know the spread in energies of a system. One measure of this spread is the standard deviation, $$\sigma_E = \sqrt{\langle E^2\rangle - \langle E \rangle^2}.$$

Show that $$\langle E^2 \rangle = \dfrac{1}{Z} \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2 Z}{\mathrm{d}\beta^2}.$$

**e)** Now use the results above to show $$\sigma_E = k_B T \sqrt{C/k_B}$$ where $$C$$ is the system's heat capacity, $$C = \dfrac{\partial \langle E \rangle }{\partial T}.$$

desc: Consider two liquids, A and B, which are insoluble (they do not mix). The pressures $$p_i$$ ($$i = A$$ or $$B$$) of their saturated vapors obey, to a good approximation, the formula $$\ln(p_i/p_0) = \dfrac{\alpha_i}{T} + \beta_i$$ where $$p_0$$ denotes the normal atmospheric…

The pressures $$p_i$$ ($$i = A$$ or $$B$$) of their saturated vapors obey, to a good approximation, the formula $$\ln(p_i/p_0) = \dfrac{\alpha_i}{T} + \beta_i$$ where $$p_0$$ denotes the normal atmospheric pressure, $$T$$ the absolute temperature of the vapor, and $$\alpha_i$$ and $$\beta_i$$ certain constants depending on the liquid.

The values of the ratio $$p_i/p_0$$ for the liquids A and B at the temperature $$40^\circ C$$ and $$90^\circ C$$ are given in the table below.

**a)** Determine the boiling temperatures of the liquids A and B under the pressure $$p_0.$$

**b)** The liquids A and B were poured into a vessel in which the layers shown in the figure below were formed. The surface of the liquid B has been covered with a thin layer of a non-volatile liquid C, which is insoluble in the liquids A and B and vice versa, thereby preventing any free evaporation from the upper surface of the liquid B. The ratio of molecular masses of the liquids A and B (in the gaseous phase) is $$\gamma = \dfrac{\mu_A}{\mu_B} = 8.$$

The masses of the liquids A and B were initially the same, each equal to $$m = 100 \;\mathrm{g}.$$ The heights of the layers of the liquids in the vessel and the densities of the liquids are small enough to make the assumption that the pressure in any point in the vessel is practically equal ot the normal atmospheric pressure $$p_0.$$

The system of liquids in the vessel is slowly, but continuously and uniformly heated. It was established that the temperature $$t$$ of the liquids changed with time $$\tau$$ as shown schematically in the figure on the right above.

Determine the temperatures $$t_1$$ and $$t_2$$ corresponding to the horizontal parts of the diagram and the masses of the liquids A and B at the time $$\tau_1.$$ The temperatures should be rounded to the nearest degree and the masses of the liquids should be determined to one tenth of a gram.

Assume that the vapors of the liquids, to a good approximation, obey the rule that the pressure of a mixture of gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of the gases forming the mixture, and that the gases can be treated as ideal.

name: In this problem, we examine the __Pound-Rebka__ experiment, conducted in 1960 by Robert…
desc: In this problem, we examine the __Pound-Rebka__ experiment, conducted in 1960 by Robert Pound and Glen Rebka Jr. This experiment was the first experimental confirmation of the __equivalence principle__, which states that holding stationary in a gravitational field is equivalent…
statement:
In this problem, we examine the __Pound-Rebka__ experiment, conducted in 1960 by Robert Pound and Glen Rebka Jr. This experiment was the first experimental confirmation of the __equivalence principle__, which states that holding stationary in a gravitational field is equivalent to accelerating at $$g$$ when there is no gravitational field.

Pound and Rebka had an iron-57 source, which they placed at the top of the Jefferson Laboratory at Harvard. They placed a second iron-57 source at the bottom of the laboratory. Gamma rays were emitted from the source at the top of the lab and absorbed by the source at the bottom of the lab. The vertical distance between the two sources was $$d = 22.5 \;\mathrm{m}.$$

When the source at the top of the lab emitted a gamma ray, it traveled down the lab to the other source at the bottom. During this time, we can think of the effect of gravity as equivalent to what would happen if the entire lab were accelerating upward at $$g.$$ Thus, it is as if the source at the bottom of the lab picked up some small speed $$v$$ moving towards the gamma ray as it fell.

(Note that gamma rays are light; they move at speed $$c.$$)

**a)** Find a simplified formula, correct to first order in $$d,$$ for the fractional shift in the wavelength $$\dfrac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda}$$ of the gamma ray as detected at the lower source when $$v/c\ll 1.$$ Your answer should be in terms of $$g, d,$$ and $$c.$$

**b)** What would be the fractional shift in wavelength in a lab on the earth's surface?

**c)** In the experiment, it was important that the sample at the bottom be able to absorb gamma rays emitted by the sample at the top. To that end, the choice of iron-57 was deliberate, as it is a useful isotope for M$$\text{\"{o}}$$ssbauer spectroscopy. When a gamma ray is emitted from an atomic nucleus, it carries momentum. To conserve momentum, the entire nucleus is kicked back in the opposite direction. However, in the M$$\text{\"{o}}$$ssbauer effect, the "kickback" momentum does not go to just the nucleus of the atom that emitted the gamma rays, but to the entire crystal in which that nucleus lies. Briefly explain why Pound and Rebka needed to use a sample that exhibits the M$$\text{\"{o}}$$ssbauer effect in their experiment.

**d)** Up until now, we have assumed that the source and target samples of iron-57 were at rest with respect to each other, as viewed from the lab frame with gravitational acceleration. In fact, in the experiment this was not the case. Instead, Pound and Rebka mounted the source on a speaker, which oscillated sinusoidally. They found that the absorption of the gamma rays oscillated as well (although not sinusoidally; the oscillation peaked once per cycle of the speaker). The peak of the absorption plot did not line up with the peak of the displacement of the speaker. Instead, they were different by some phase $$\phi.$$ Find $$\phi$$ in terms of $$A,$$ the amplitude of speaker oscillations, $$f,$$ the frequency of the speaker oscillations, and $$g, d,$$ and $$c.$$

name: This problem continues discussion of the equivalence principle, which we began in the…
desc: This problem continues discussion of the equivalence principle, which we began in the previous problem on the Pound-Rebka experiment. Another consequence of the equivalence principle is that light will be bent in a gravitational field. This has never been measured on the surface…
statement:
This problem continues discussion of the equivalence principle, which we began in the previous problem on the Pound-Rebka experiment.

Another consequence of the equivalence principle is that light will be bent in a gravitational field. This has never been measured on the surface of the Earth, but was verified qualitatively by Arthur Eddington by observing starlight passing near the sun's edge during a total eclipse in 1919. (Eddington needed to wait for a solar eclipse because this was the only time it was possible to observe the position in the sky of stars whose light passed close by the sun.)

In this problem, we ask why the observation can't practically be done on earth's surface.

Let's predict how much bending we should see in a laboratory at rest on the earth's surface. What one would observe in such a laboratory should be the same as what one would observe in a laboratory accelerating in deep space with a uniform acceleration of $$\vec{a} = -\vec{g},$$ where $$\vec{g}$$ is the acceleration due to gravity on Earth's surface.

Imagine that a laser at one end of the laboratory emits a beam of light that originally travels parallel to the laboratory floor. This light shines on the opposite wall of the laboratory a horizontal distance $$d = 30.0 \;\mathrm{m}$$ away from the laser.

**a)** Find the magnitude of this deflection in a laboratory on the surface of the earth.

**b)** Find the magnitude of this deflection if the laboratory sits on the surface of a neutron star with mass $$M = 3.0 \times 10^{30} \;\mathrm{kg}$$ and a radius of $$R = 12 \;\mathrm{km}.$$

statement:
**a)** When an electron annihilates with a positron (the antiparticle of an electron, having all the same properties as an electron, but with opposite charge), photons are produced. Explain why it is not possible for this process to produce a single photon only.

**b)** A positron moving with velocity $$v$$ in the positive $$x$$ direction annihilates with a stationary electron, producing two identical photons. Find the angle between the emitted photons in terms of $$\gamma_v = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}.$$

**c)** Fluorine-18 undergoes beta-plus decay and is commonly used in positron emission tomography. Positrons are emitted with a range of kinetic energies up to a maximum of $$635 \;\mathrm{keV}.$$ If a positron were to immediately annihilate with an electron, producing two photons, what would be the minimum angle between them?

Below is a spacetime diagram showing two worldlines. Also shown in dots are hyperbolas which connect spacetime points that all have the same invariant interval, $$\Delta s^2 = \Delta x^2 - c \Delta t^2,$$ from the origin (labeled $$0).$$

desc: Some elements have radioactive isotopes (radioisotopes) which can be used for medical imaging. A radioisotope is injected into the bloodstream, whence it is taken up by organs in the body. Areas of extremely high cell growth or repair such as tumors take up and retain this…
statement:
Some elements have radioactive isotopes (radioisotopes) which can be used for medical imaging. A radioisotope is injected into the bloodstream, whence it is taken up by organs in the body. Areas of extremely high cell growth or repair such as tumors take up and retain this isotope much more efficiently than any other tissue. Thus, imaging using radioisotopes can be used to indicate malignant tissue growth.

Technetium--99m ($${}^{99m}\mathrm{Tc}$$) is one such radioisotope. It is used for imaging organs such as the thyroid, liver, kidneys, and brain. The half life of this isotope is $$\tau_{1/2} = 6.01 \;\mathrm{h}.$$

Rates of radioactivity can be measured in Curies (Ci), equivalent to $$3.7 \times 10^{10}$$ decays per second.

In this question, we examine a model of the process of $${}^{99mc}\mathrm{Tc}$$ uptake in a patient's cancerous thyroid glands. The patient is an otherwise healthy adult. In this model, $$A = 10.0 \;\mathrm{mCi}$$ of $${}^{99m}\mathrm{Tc}$$ is injected into a vein in the patient's arm. The radius of the vein is $$1.00 \;\mathrm{mm}.$$ The radioisotope enters the bloodstream, then enters each thyroid gland through an artery in the patient's neck. The radius of this artery is $$1.70 \;\mathrm{mm}.$$

Let the velocities of blood flow in the partient's arm and neck be $$v_a = 3.00 \;\mathrm{mm/s}$$ and $$v_n = 40.0 \;\mathrm{cm/s}.$$ Let the total blood volume of the patient be $$V = 5 \;\mathrm{L},$$ and let each thyroid gland (there are two) have volume $$V_t = 9 \;\mathrm{mL}.$$

The $${}^{99m}\mathrm{Tc}$$ emits gamma rays of energy $$E = 2.24 \times 10^{-14} \;\mathrm{J}.$$

**a)** What is the concentration (in number of atoms per liter) of $${}^{99m}\mathrm{Tc}$$ in the bloodstream after the injection?

**b)** Qualitatively, sketch the amount of $${}^{99m}\mathrm{Tc}$$ in the thyroid as a function of time, starting from the time of injection.

**c)** The continuity equation in fluid mechanics states that the volume flow rate of fluid flowing through a pipe is constant. Consider the blood flow in the arm and neck of the patient. Does the continuity equation hold in this model? Explain why or why not.

**d)** What is the initial rate of energy release due to gamma radiation emitted from a thyroid gland? In this and subsequent parts you may neglect the time taken for the thyroid glands to saturate with $${}^{99m}\mathrm{Tc}.$$

**e)** A scan is taken over $$t_s = 10.0 \;\mathrm{min}.$$ If the total energy detected by the scanner exceeds $$E_{\rm min} = 5\times 10^{-4} \;\mathrm{J},$$ an image appears due to radioactivity in the thyroid gland. Approximately how much time will elapse before radioactivity is no longer detected in a scan?

At very high temperatures (as in the early universe), the proton and the neutron can be thought of as two different states of the same particle, called the __nucleon__. (The reactions that convert a proton to a neutron or vice versa require the absorption of an electron or a positron or a neutrino, but all of these particles tend to very abundant at sufficiently high temperatures.)

Since the neutron's mass is higher than the proton's by $$2.3 \times 10^{-30} \;\mathrm{kg},$$ its energy is higher by this amount times $$c^2.$$ Suppose, that at some very early time, the nucleons were in thermal equilibrium with the rest of the universe at $$10^{11} \;\mathrm{K}.$$ What fraction of the nucleons at that time were protons, and what fraction were neutrons?

statement:
A nucleus contains $$N$$ neutrons and $$Z$$ protons. It therefore contains $$A = N+Z$$ nucleons.

The mass, $$M(A,N,Z)$$ can be approximated using the __semi-empirical mass formula__: $$M(A,Z) \approx N m_n + Z m_p - a_a A + a_2 A^{2/3} + a_3 Z^2 A^{-1/3} + a_4(A - 2Z)^2 A^{-1} + a_5 \delta(A,Z)$$ where \begin{aligned} a_1 & = 15.8 \;\mathrm{MeV}/c^2 \\ a_2 & = 18.3 \;\mathrm{MeV}/c^2 \\ a_3 & = 0.714 \;\mathrm{MeV}/c^2 \\ a_4 & = 23.2 \;\mathrm{MeV}/c^2 \\ a_5 & = 12 \;\mathrm{MeV}/c^2 \end{aligned} and $$ \delta(A,Z) = \begin{cases} -A^{-1/2}; \;\; \text{ Z and N are odd} \\ A^{1/2}; \;\; \text{ Z and N are even} \\ 0; \;\; \text{A is odd} \end{cases} $$

The model is partly based on theory and partly based on experiment. $$A$$ and $$Z$$ are taken to vary continuously in this model.

**a)** Find an expression for the binding energy of the nucleus. The $$\delta(A,Z)$$ terms captures the tendency of nucleons to form pairs in the nucleus, so is often referred to as the "pairing" term. Give a brief explanation of the origin of the other terms in the equation. Your goal is not to look these up, but to your understanding of the functional forms and the places that energy might come from to conjecture what each term means.

**b)** The term in equation which has a constant $$a_3$$ in front is often written as $$a_3 Z(Z-1) A^{-1/3}.$$ Suggest why this might be.

**c)** Represent the binding energy graphically as a function of $$Z$$ for a given mass number, justifying your reasoning.

statement:
Planck's blackbody radiation law says that the power per unit surface radiated by a convex black body at temperature $$T$$ between the wavelengths $$\lambda$$ and $$\lambda + \mathrm{d}\lambda$$ is $$W(\lambda, T) = \dfrac{2\pi c^2 h}{\lambda^5\left(e^{hc/(\lambda k_B T)} - 1\right)}.$$

In this problem we do a couple of basic calculations with this law; in the next two problems we see where it comes from.

**a)** Find the total power emitted per unit surface area. The result is called the __Stefan-Boltzmann law__, and often written $$\sigma T^4,$$ where $$\sigma$$ is the __Stefan-Boltzmann constant__. Express $$\sigma$$ in terms of other fundamental constants.

You may use the result $$\int_0^\infty \dfrac{x^3}{e^x - 1}\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{\pi^4}{15}.$$

**b)** Wien's displacement law says that the wavelength where the spectrum peaks is given by $$\lambda_{\rm peak} = \dfrac{b}{T}.$$ Find $$b,$$ finding the value of any constants involved to three significant figures.

statement:
In this problem and the next, we derive Planck's blackbody radiation law, combining results from quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics. You may want to review the problems on the partition function from our statistical mechanics class before working this problem.

**a)** Consider a one-dimensional box of length $$L.$$ Inside the box are photons. These behave as quantum particles in a box. What are the allowed wavelengths, momenta, and energies of the photons? Give your answer in terms of fundamental constants and $$n,$$ the quantum number of the photon. ($$n=1$$ in the lowest allowed mode.)

**b)** Find the partition function for the box at temperature $$T.$$

**c)** Find the average energy $$\bar{E}$$ of the box at temperature $$T.$$

**d)** Next we consider a three-dimensional box. A photon in this box has three quantum numbers: $$n_x, n_y,$$ and $$n_z.$$ You can think of its wavefunction as multiplying three wavefunctions together - one for each dimension of the box. Find the energy of a photon in terms of $$n_x, n_y,$$ and $$n_z.$$

**e)** Suppose we wanted to find the total energy inside the box. To do this, we take the average energy in each mode and integrate over all the modes. Although the modes are discrete, we can approximate them as continuous with the integral $$U = 2\int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \bar{E}(n_x,n_y,n_z) \mathrm{d}n_x \mathrm{d}n_x \mathrm{d}n_z.$$

We have included an extra factor of $$2$$ to account for the two independent polarization states of a photon.

To actually carry out this integral, we convert to spherical coordinates, obtaining $$U = \int_0^\infty \mathrm{d}n \int_0^{\pi/2} \mathrm{d}\theta \int_0^{\pi/2} \mathrm{d}\phi n^2 \sin \theta \bar{E}(n).$$

Find $$U/V,$$ the energy per unit volume in the box.

**f)** Find the entropy of this "photon gas".

**g)** For the integral in part (e), perform just the integrals over $$\theta$$ and $$\phi$$ to obtain a one-dimensional integral over $$n.$$ Change variables to $$\epsilon,$$ the energy of a photon.

The resulting integrand is denoted $$u(\epsilon),$$ it is the energy density per unit photon energy inside the box. Find $$u(\epsilon).$$

**h)** Suppose a small hole of area $$a$$ is poked in the box. What is the power per unit wavelength, $$\lambda,$$ that comes out of the hole? (This involves two parts - studying the kinematics of the photons to see how many escape the hole per unit time, and switching variables from photon energy to wavelength.) Your result black body radiation law.

**i)** Give an argument from thermodynamics that an ideal black body must radiate in the same way as the hole in the box full of photons.
